messages.subject: DISTANCE question
messages.body_plain:
Hello.
  I was hoping someone could help me with a conceptual problem I'm having
with DISTANCE.I conducted a line transect survey of chimpanzee and gorilla
nests in CAR last year. We walked about 140 km of transects. I am now trying
to analyze density using DISTANCE. Basically, we would walk along and upon
seeing nests from the transects, search the forest surrounding the transect
(approx. 30 m or so) looking for any additional nests. All nests that were
found either via sighting from the transect or subsequent search were
recorded, and distances from one another ( and the transect) were written
down. No prior transect width (w) had been used, although for the most part
we walked along in a straight line down the transect. Currently, I am ready
to enter the data into DISTANCE for analysis, but I am unsure of how I
should determine what my strip width is (and hence which nest clusters to
exlude from analysis). Here is my plan - can anyone tell me if I am doing
the right thing?
  I placed each group of nests dating from the same time period and within
50 m of one another in one 'cluster'. DISTANCE says I should find the
mid-point of each cluster and if it falls within w (strip width) then I
should include all of the nests (those visible from transect and those not)
in the analysis. But how do I determine the initial strip width? To do THAT
i intend to first enter in to DISTANCE (NOT under cluster format) all nests
seen from the transect on all the transects...in other words, enter each
nest visible from the transect into DISTANCE individually (using grouped
categories, i.e. 0-5 m, 6-10 m,11-15 m, etc). I am hoping that DISTANCE will
then calculate for me the point at which percentage of nests visible from
the transect drops down to 15% of the transect center (another option would
be to delete 5% of the outliers, correct?). I s this the right approach?
This will give me my w width. THEN, having finished all of this, I will
enter the nest clusters into DISTANCE, only counting the ones whose
midpoints fall into the above-determined w. Then DISTANCE will be able to
calculate for me the density. Is this correct? Or can someone think of a
better approach?
  Also, there are several different forest types in my study regon, some
more dense than others. Should I calculate w separately for each? For
chimpanzees there are over a hundred nest sites, but for gorillas there are
~15. So, for gorillas, is there a big enough sample size to split them into
forest type, or should I find the w of all lumped together? What do you
think?
  I would really appreciate any input on this. I want to analyze my data
correctly, and as the Buckland book does not address my specific situation,
I was hoping for someone's help.
  Thank you very much,

Sincerely,
                                                                    Cleve
Hicks

messages.subject: Re: DISTANCE question
messages.body_plain:
Cleve, yes, analyse your data initially without truncation.  You may find
you don't need to truncate any data (in which case Distance takes w as the
largest distance in your data), but generally, you gain some robustness by
truncation, as the model doesn't have to fit the tail of the
distribution.  So either 5% or g(w)=0.15 may work well, but don't feel you
have to use either - truncate the smallest amount that allows you to fit a
good model to the data.

SE means standard error.  If your nest production rate is exactly 1, this
will be zero, so enter it as zero.  If this is 1 per day, then make sure
your mean time to disappearance is recorded in days.  Your data on
disappearance should allow you to calculate a std error on this quantity,
which you can enter.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: setting filter
messages.body_plain:
Hi Cleve, list,

You can do it a similar way to the way you describe: have two observation
layers, one for each species -- but I think the following is simpler.

Add a new field to the observation layer, and call it Species or something like
that.  Then in your observation layer, have all the records for both species,
with the species field being c for chimp and g for gorilla nest.  So, for
example, if on a transect I saw 3 chimp nests and 2 gorilla nests the
observation layer might be:

   Perp. distance          Species
      2.45                  c
      9.34                  c
      1.87                  c
      9.55                  g
      0.23                  g

This is generally how people store the stuff in spreadsheets so should be pretty
easy to import into Distance.

In the analysis stage, you then need to set up two data filters, one to select
only the "c"s and the other to select the "g"s.  For example,for your chimp only
analysis, there would be a line in the Data Selection tab of the data filter
that would state Layer type Observation and Selection criteria species="c"

Hope this helps -- email me at dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk if you need more help
with the program use -- although we're teaching distance workshops for the next
couple of weeks so I might be a little slow to respond.

I didn't understand quite what you wanted to do with the strata so I can't
respond there without more details.

I also don't quite see what you thought Steve said about the chosen w being
larger than the effective strip halfwidth.  The ESW is a function of the w you
choose: if you see everything within w then the ESW is equal to w.  Generally,
if you see a proportion P_a of the animals within w then ESW=w P_a.  This is on
page 53 of Introduction to Distance sampling (I found it by looking for
Effective Strip Width in the index at the back).

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Re: comparing EDR values
messages.body_plain:
> > I'm interested in assessing the statistical significance of the difference
> > in species-specific effective detection radii (EDR) derived from point
> > count data in two different habitats.  Can anyone give me any pointers on
> > how to do this?

One simple way, though based on information criteria rather than
significance testing, is to define two strata in Distance, corresponding
to the 2 habitats.  Then fit your chosen model for the detection function,
a) selecting the 'global option', which fits a single detection function
to the data from both habitats, and b) selecting the option of fitting a
separate detection function by stratum (see estimate tab in model defn).
Compare the AIC value from a) with the sum of the 2 AIC values from
b).  If the latter is smaller than the former, assume that the 2 habitats
have different effective radii.  This approach is described in the 2001
distance sampling book.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: pygmy nuthatch detection function
messages.body_plain:
Nicole,

Here is an attempt to take some workload off Len and Steve.

One of my favorite slogans is "You need clay to make bricks."  I would
advise against making inferences from your sample of 10.  Especially given
the gregarious nature of these critters.  Were all ten observations on the
same point?  Distance sampling in the presence of strong spatial
aggregation requires even more data than in more uniformly distributed
animals (cluster size analysis notwithstanding).

Even if someone reports that their pygmy nuthatch observations fit a
hazard-rate (or any other) function, it has no relevance to your study.
The detection process is partly due to the species "innate" sightability
(behavior, color, etc.), partly due to the the condtions under which
sampling took place (habitat, weather, etc.), and partly due to the
observer herself (experience, interest, eye sight and hearing ability,
etc.).  Thus, do nut expect a "pygmy nuthatch" detection function.

Your best bet is to use what data you do have.  The advantage of using
surrogate species in your study is that, at least, they may have
environmental and observer effects in common.  Use your a priori knowledge
of similarities (in detectability) among species, and model selection
statistics, to find the best pooling.  Assuming a detection function for
the species, it seems to me, is a poor strategy.

Good luck,
Aaron Ellingson

messages.subject: Trapping webs
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance List,

I'm after some advice on trapping webs. Myself and a colleague are
trying to design a sampling protocol for the estimation of mongoose
density in Madagascar. The trapping web approach has the huge advantage
of enabling a distance based estimation of density, and a mark -
recapture estimate to be derived from the same data set, and so we would
very much like to use this.

A problem we may face is one of scale. Little is known of the home range
size, but estimates vary between 17ha - 200ha, this depends on group
size. This gives a radius of a circular home range of between 232m -
797m. If we placed traps at these distances the total area could be
between 11 sq km - 128 sq km (assuming eight traps per spoke). This of
course could be totally un-workable. We were wondering whether a
fractional approach could be possible. Where a segment of the trapping
circle is used, for instance a quarter. The effort is then entered in
the analysis stage as 0.25 and obviously multiplied by the number of
trapping sessions. We already use this approach in some other point
transect work we carry out. There is at least one problem we can see
with this. (I'm sure there are many more!) and that is the incursion of
animals from outside of the trapping area. In a full trapping web the
data can be truncated to allow for this behaviour, in effect a buffer
zone. Obviously for a segment there are three edges to consider as
opposed to just the one in a circle. Would it be possible to buffer trap
all three edges?

I guess the simple answer to this problem may be that the home ranges
are simply too big and therefore a different method should be employed.
We're fairly sure that line transects would be impractical due to the
density of the undergrowth and the mobility of the animals. Any other
suggestions?

The other problem (there always is another one!) is the variation in the
group sizes. Anywhere between 1 and 13 individuals. Obviously multiple
traps at points could help with this, but of course this raises the
issue of cluster size. Sixty to eighty "observations" would be the
target, but is an observation a individual capture, or 60-80 captures of
one or more?

Any advice on this would be very welcome. Thanks in advance.

Tim.

messages.subject: Re: Trapping webs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tim, list

Sounds like a hard problem indeed.

Yes, I should think you could buffer trap all 3 edges of the web, but you're
going to end up losing a large amount of data this way as your edge to inside
ratio will be high.

Instead of a trapping web you could perhaps consider a trapping line, where the
traps are laid at varying density perpendicular to a line, with the aim of
catching all animals on the line and less off the line.   This is detailed in
Chapter 9 of the Advanced Distance Sampling book we're currently preparing (the
chapter's lead author is Paul Lukacs - I'm cc'ing this to him in case he has
additional comments) -- if you email Steve Buckland he may be able to send you a
draft.  Trapping lines may offer better precision relative to trapping webs in
the same way that line transects tend to be more precise than point transects
for the same number of observations.

You can simulate trapping webs and lines to look at potential biases using
software Paul has written - see
http://www.colostate.edu/depts/coopunit/paul-lukacs/web.html

A big problem with passive distance sampling methods is that movement can cause
big biases, and so the trap spacing has to be optimized for the target animal.
An alternative approach that uses information from recaptured animals to
estimate movement for arbitrary trap spacings has been developed by Murray
Efford, and software is available at
http://www.landcareresearch.co.nz/services/software/density/

You may be able to to use a trapping web or line setup in conjunction with
Murray's estimation approach.

If groups vary from 1 to 13 I think you're liable to get into serious problems
if you need to assume that you catch all animals in a group at the line/point.
Do you really think you'll catch all 13 mongeese (is that the right plural) in
13 adjacent traps on a line?

However I'm struggling to be able to suggest alternatives.  I guess they don't
leave sign that is linearly related to density -- such as scats?  You could then
use indirect methods (you'd need to estimate scat production rate and
disappearance time) with either line transects or strip transects.

Perhaps someone else can come up with alternative suggestions?

(In terms of sample size for estimating the detection function it is the number
of clusters not the number of individuals -- but I think that's the least of
your worries!).

Cheers,

 - Len

messages.subject: Re: error messages
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joan, list:

The forrtl: error messages come from the analysis engine, which is written in
FORTRAN.  The output conversion error messages probably indicate a minor bug in
the program where some value it was trying to write to a file is longer than it
anticipated (e.g., an integer value of 1000 was being written in a space that only
had 3 characters reserved for it).  The floating underflow error can safely be
ignored.  I'm surprised that you got no estimates at all on account of these
errors.  Anyway, send me a copy of your distance project and I'll check it out.

A general note to anyone sending distance projects to me (or anyone else): do not
just send the .dst file -- a project is composed of the project file (.dst) and
the project folder (.dat) (See online help, chapter 4).  The best way to send them
is to use the Distance menu option File | Export Project... and then choose .zip
under "Save as".  This packs both the project file and project folder into a .zip
file.  For more, look in the online help index under "Exporting projects".

Cheers,

 - Len

messages.subject: chimpanzee nest project
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,
   I am hoping to get input on a question about my data analysis. I carried
out line transect surveys for chimp and gorilla nests in Ngotto Forest. My
team walked down the transect, and when we spotted a nest (or nests) we
would then do a rough search on both sides of the transect for any other
nests in the group. We would record the distance of each nest off the
transect and with the help of Frank Verret and Len Thomas I have come up
with an ESW of ~1m for the chimps and ~6 m for the gorillas (8 m and 5 m
with truncation). I have become worried, however, in that I am actually
losing a lot of nest sites (particularly chimp nest sites) who have outlier
nests falling far off the transect, which tend to pull the site's midpoint
out far from the transect Many of the larger chimp nest sites have several
nests (usually not visible from the trail) that were found 35, 40 or even 50
m from the transect. I think I erred in not cutting off our search area on
either side of the transect at, say, 20 m. We searched both sides of the
transect to some degree, but when we saw nests on one side of the trail we
would spend much time measuring the nests and trees on that side, and thus
were more likely to spot other nests further in that direction, and thus
sometimes we were led up to 50 m away from the transect counting nests. We
did not search an equivalent distance on the other side of the transect.
And I think this is giving me some real outliers that are resulting in the
midpoints far from the transect (outside the ESW) and I am losing data. What
I want to know is: at this point, would I be justified in limiting the nests
used in my analysis to only those found within, say, 20 m of the transect on
either side? Any nests we found by searching beyond this distance would thus
be excluded. I really think this is the solution to my difficulty, but if
anybody sees any flaws in this, please let me know! Thanks!
      Cleve Hicks
